BackfillChainRequest.description:
Narrowing for a chain backfill.

`limit` caps how many items join the queue in one call. It exists because
this verb is the one that queues fetches of third-party pages (issue
#35): the default is a conservative batch, and an operator who wants a
longer run asks for it explicitly rather than discovering it as a burst
at someone's blog. Repeat the call to continue — queuing is idempotent.
BackfillChainRequest.title: BackfillChainRequest

DeleteItemsRequest.description:
Ids to delete, and nothing else.

A list rather than a filter. A filter reads as a convenient way to say
"everything matching this", which is exactly the blast radius this
operation should not have; a caller wanting a whole source cleared names
the source endpoint, where that intent is explicit.
DeleteItemsRequest.title: DeleteItemsRequest

DeleteSourceItemsRequest.description:
Narrowing for a per-source item deletion.

Every field is optional: an empty body means "everything this source
collected", which is the common case after a bad crawl.
DeleteSourceItemsRequest.title: DeleteSourceItemsRequest

IngestItem.description:
One item an agent is pushing into an agent source (ADR 0022).

Deliberately *not* ItemDraft, which carries `source_id`. Binding that
directly is how the endpoint this replaces let a write-scoped caller
inject items into any source, including ones it does not own. The field
is absent here so the privilege line holds at the type level: there is no
key to send, so no runtime check can be forgotten.
IngestItem.title: IngestItem

IngestRequest.description:
Body for pushing items into an agent source.

The cap is body-parsing hygiene rather than per-source rate limiting
(which ADR 0022 explicitly declines to add): at 1 MiB per request an
uncapped list admits thousands of title-only items in one call, and each
one costs a dedupe lookup and possibly an enrichment row.
IngestRequest.title: IngestRequest

ItemSort.description:
The sortable orders, whitelisted rather than free-form.

An arbitrary column name here would either fail at the database or, if
interpolated, become an injection point — SQL identifiers cannot be passed
as query parameters.
ItemSort.title: ItemSort

PublishStatus.description:
Lifecycle of an Item with respect to external visibility (C5).

The gate is the point: because NetNewsWire caches whatever it fetched
first, an item must not appear in a feed until every processor in its
chain has succeeded. `published` is terminal for the item's content.
PublishStatus.title: PublishStatus

SourceBatchCreate.description:
Body for creating several sources in one request.

Shared options apply to every URL. `type` may be `'auto'`, resolved per URL
against the collectors exactly as the single endpoint's callers resolve it,
so there is no per-item type field to keep in step.

The list is validated for shape only. Whether a URL is usable *for its
type* is decided per item by the handler, because one bad entry must fail
alone rather than refuse the batch (ADR 0044).
SourceBatchCreate.title: SourceBatchCreate

SourceCreate.description:
Body for creating a source.

`pipeline_chain` + `target_lang` enable the processing chain at creation
time — the correct ordering: first source with chain, then first fetch,
so no item is ever cached unprocessed.
SourceCreate.title: SourceCreate

SourceFetchItem.description:
Body for fetching one address into one source.

The atom the plural forms are built from: `:fetch-items` loops it, and a
`kind=fetch` work runs it once per target. It carries no pacing knobs
because there is nothing to pace: one address is one request.
SourceFetchItem.title: SourceFetchItem

SourceFetchItems.description:
Body for fetching a caller's addresses into one source.

`urls` are addresses the caller discovered -- an agent enumerating a
site's history, typically -- and every one of them must be on the source's
own host, or it is refused rather than fetched.

The two knobs shape the pacing: `batch_size` addresses are fetched, then a
pause of `min_interval_seconds`. Both are clamped by the server, and the
deployment's own interval (PEARSS_FETCH_MIN_INTERVAL) is a floor under
them, so a caller cannot ask this deployment to hit someone's server
harder than the operator allows.
SourceFetchItems.title: SourceFetchItems

SourcePatch.description:
Body for updating a source. Absent fields are left alone.

`pipeline_chain` is a JSON list of {plugin_id, kind, lang?, required?}
specs the source's items must complete before the gate opens; an explicit
`null` clears the chain (items go ready straight after normalisation).
Absent vs explicit-null is decided by `model_fields_set`, the pydantic v2
way to give PATCH bodies three-state fields.
SourcePatch.title: SourcePatch

SourceStatus.description:
Lifecycle of a content source.

There is no `deleted`. Deletion removes the row (ADR 0021), and a status
meaning "this row is really gone" cannot describe a row that exists --
keeping one invited every reader to handle a state that was never durable.
SourceStatus.title: SourceStatus

TrustLevel.description:
Recorded operator intent about a source.

The hard rule, from docs/domain/data-model.md: this never makes fetched
content trusted. A `trusted` source's body is still untrusted input —
AGENTS.md is explicit that external pages and RSS bodies must never be
treated as instructions, and a per-source flag that silently flipped that
would be the most dangerous possible reading of the field.

Nothing currently branches on this value. It is stored and surfaced so the
distinction exists in the data before any behaviour depends on it; giving
it effects requires an ADR, because the only behaviour it could plausibly
change is a security default.
TrustLevel.title: TrustLevel

post.description:
Exchange credentials for an auth token.

Returns the auth token in the three-field form clients expect. Never
reveals whether the username or the password was the wrong part.

Remove a folder -- Read You's group delete.

Read You deletes a group's feeds first (`deleteFeed` per feed) and then
calls this. Since a folder is a value on the sources rather than a row,
"removing" it means moving its sources back to the default folder: the
group stops existing because nothing carries its name any more, and the
subscriptions inside it survive rather than vanishing with it.

Refusing when sources remain would be defensible, but it would break the
client's intent: it has already unsubscribed the feeds it meant to, and
a refusal here leaves the remainder in a folder the user just deleted.

Mark items read/unread and starred/unstarred.

Idempotent by construction: the same request replayed produces the same
state, because every write is last-write-wins on a fixed pair of flags.
Mark everything in a stream read up to a timestamp.

Rename a folder -- Read You's group rename.

Folders in Pearss are not entities: a source carries a `folder` name and
the set of folders is derived from those names (`tag/list` reads them
back with a DISTINCT). So renaming is a rename of the *value*, applied to
every source that carries it, and an empty folder needs no handling
because an empty folder does not exist.

Both ids arrive as `user/-/label/<name>` streams. A `dest` that is not a
label stream is a client bug worth refusing rather than guessing at.

Content for specific items.

Authenticated like a read, not like a write. This endpoint changes nothing
-- it is POST only because the item ids are too numerous for a query
string -- and NetNewsWire sends it with the Authorization header and no
form `T`. Requiring `T` here returned 401 to every real client request,
which surfaced as a populated article list whose bodies were all blank.

schema.title: Response Stream Items Contents Api Greader Php Reader Api 0 Stream Items Contents Post

get.description:
Item ids for a stream.

`c` is a continuation cursor: the reply carries `continuation` while more
items remain, and the client follows it. That is part of the protocol,
not an optimisation -- a client that cannot page can only ever see the
first page, and it has no way to tell a truncated answer from a complete
one. Read You's `fetchItemIdsAndContinue` loops `while continuation !=
null`, so omitting the cursor made it treat the first 1000 ids as the
whole read set, which is how a read item marked in another client failed
to propagate.

`xt` excludes a state, `it` includes one -- both are how a client fetches
a subset, and both are applied in SQL so `n` bounds the *answer* rather
than the pre-filter set. That ordering is load-bearing: Read You asks for
"the newest 1000 unread", and filtering after a limit would hand it fewer
than it asked for, which it counts as items that do not exist.

FreshRSS clients express the read stream with `it=`, not `s=`. Read You
sends `s=reading-list&it=<read>` for a FreshRSS account and `s=<read>` for
a Google Reader one (`useIt = isFreshRss` in its source). Ignoring `it`
made that query return the whole library -- and because the client reads
the result as "these are read", it marked every unread item read on each
sync, while a parallel branch flipped them back. The unread count
oscillated between 0 and the total.

The page size bounds the *answer*, so a short page is meaningful: if
fewer ids come back than were asked for, the stream is exhausted. That is
what lets the cursor below be a plain offset rather than something the
client has to interpret -- it never has to compare pages, only to keep
asking while a cursor is offered.

Pending items are always excluded: the gate applies to the Reader API just
as it does to RSS.

`ot` is a lower bound on `published_at`, in Unix seconds. ReadYou sends it
on every global sync (`getReadItemIds(since = now - 1 month)`) and pages to
exhaustion, so honouring it bounds the walk to the window the client asked
for instead of the whole read history.

schema.title: Response Stream Items Ids Api Greader Php Reader Api 0 Stream Items Ids Get

post.description:
Move, rename and remove subscriptions -- the app's management writes.

FreshRSS's contract: `ac=edit`, `s` names the feeds, `a` a label to add,
`r` one to remove, `t` a new title. A feed can only be in one category,
so an `a` wins and the folder is set; an `r` without an `a` moves back to
the default. Unknown feeds are skipped rather than 404'd, the same
leniency edit-tag applies to item ids -- a client works from the ids
subscription/list gave it, and one that was withdrawn since should not
fail the whole edit.

`t=` renames the source. It was refused silently until 2026-09-16, on
the reasoning that the next fetch would overwrite the name; reading
`set_source_title_if_absent` shows that reasoning was wrong -- the
conditional write fills an absent title and never replaces a present
one, exactly to protect an operator's rename. A client rename is that
same choice expressed from an app, so it now lands through the same
guarded write and sticks (ADR 0024, revision).

`ac=unsubscribe` deletes the source with everything it collected -- the
ADR 0021 semantics, through the same repository entry point
`DELETE /v1/sources` uses. It was refused outright for a day; the
refusal was reversed because refusing a client whose UI already showed
a confirmation dialog achieved nothing except a permanent retry loop
(`deleteFeed` failing reads as sync failure). The delete is real and
irreversible, as it is through `/v1`; a replay answers OK rather than
an error, matching the "already gone is done" rule the /v1 endpoint
established. `ac=subscribe` stays unsupported: subscribing goes through
`quickadd`, which is what the one client that subscribes actually
calls.

schema.title: Response Subscription List Api Greader Php Reader Api 0 Subscription List Get
Response Subscription List Api Greader Php Reader Api 0 Subscription List Post

post.description:
Subscribe to a feed URL -- Read You's "add feed" path.

The URL arrives already resolved. Read You fetches the address the user
typed, parses it, follows any `<link rel=alternate>` to the actual feed,
and only then calls this with the *feed's* URL (`RssHelper.searchFeed` ->
`discoverFeedLink`, then `subscribe(feedLink = resolvedFeedLink)`). So
this is not a discovery endpoint: it subscribes to what it is given, and
A5 `discover_feed` -- deferred by decision, not by omission -- stays
deferred.

What it does share with discovery is the failure mode worth guarding: the
client `requireNotNull`s `streamId` and lets the exception escape into
`sync`, whose catch answers `Result.retry()`. An endpoint that returned
no id would therefore not fail one "add feed" -- it would put the whole
account into a retry loop. Hence a real subscription and a real id, or an
error, never a well-formed empty reply.

Idempotent by the identity of the source: re-adding a URL returns the
existing subscription, which is what `create_source` already does for the
same reason (`POST /v1/sources` relies on it).

schema.title: Response Subscription Quickadd Api Greader Php Reader Api 0 Subscription Quickadd Post

get.description:
Starred state plus the folders that exist.

A client builds its sidebar from this and from the categories on
subscription/list; the two must agree about which folders exist or the
sidebar shows groups with nothing in them (or subscriptions with no
group). Folders are derived from the sources, so an empty folder simply
does not appear -- there is no folder entity of its own to persist.

Response User Info Api Greader Php Reader Api 0 User Info Post

get.description:
Liveness probe: no dependency on the database.

The HTTP process being alive says nothing about the background
loops (A07): a scheduler killed by an escaped error used to leave
this returning ok forever. Started workers report their task
liveness here; a dead loop degrades the answer to 503 with the
offender named, so monitoring sees the degradation instead of
quietly stopped collection.

post.description:
Requeue one failed chain row -- and only that row.

The granularity the source-scoped route lacks. A source can hold 23
permanently failed products while the caller wants three of them retried
(measured: that was all-or-nothing), and the row is addressable --
`list_enrichments` returns its id -- so the command can name it.

Only `failed` rows are requeued. A `queued` or `running` row is already on
its way, so this answers the same 200 with `requeued: 0`: the request means
"make sure this row will be attempted", and that is already true. A
`succeeded` row is a 409 -- its product exists, and producing it again is a
different command -- while an id naming nothing is a 404.

What a requeue *means* lives in one place (`requeue_enrichment`), which is
also what the source-scoped route calls once per failed row: the attempt
budget restarts and the stale failure is cleared, while `input_hash` stays,
because the content has not changed.

get.description:
List collected items, newest first by default.

Two ways to search, and they answer different questions: `q` is a substring
match on the title, and `full_text` is a real search over titles and bodies
(ADR 0035). `full_text` with `sort=relevance` ranks by FTS5's bm25; without
it the matches keep the time order and its keyset cursor.

Bodies are not included at any `fields` setting; fetch them from
`/v1/items/{id}/body`. Pending items never appear.

delete.description:
Delete one item, permanently.

Removes the row, its stored body, its read state and its processor
products. Not reversible and not a hide: the content is gone, and the
client's cached copy is the only one left (ADR 0021).

An id naming nothing answers 200 with `items: 0`, not 404 -- see
delete_source for why a retry must be indistinguishable from the first.

get.description: One item, without its body.

The item's body, as its own request.

Separate by design: docs/api/style-guide.md forbids inlining HTML bodies in
list responses, and the architecture routes large content through an
explicit reference so a caller pays for it only when it asks.

Serving a body is an observable first publication (ADR 0016: with the
public RSS render removed, this and the Reader API are the paths where a
client actually sees content), so the item's content is frozen here — the
immutability guarantee exists because clients cache what they were shown.

Items that look like another copy of this one (AC-109).

A hint, and only a hint. The measurement behind the threshold puts a copy and
a genuine paraphrase 0.014 apart, so no threshold can be right about that gap;
what this endpoint can honestly say is "these two are close", and what to do
about it is the caller's decision (ADR 0021: deletion belongs to the user).
Nothing here merges, deletes, rewrites or re-keys anything.

Why *this* item is being held: its processor-chain rows, and nothing else.

The dimension the source-scoped route lacks. An agent that already has an
item id (from search_items) had to list its whole source's chain rows and
filter them in context -- the shape the guide's "filter on the server" rule
exists to avoid -- and it needed a title search first, which can come back
empty for the very item it is holding (issue #72).

A *pending* item is answered, unlike every other item read. The gate hides
content, and these rows are the reason the content is held -- answering 404
here would make the route useless for exactly the question it exists for (a
chain that failed and left an item stuck). The source-scoped route already
returned these rows for a source's pending items, so this is the consistent
choice rather than a new exception; `detail` carries the processor's own
error text, which is metadata about the attempt rather than the item.

An id that names nothing is still 404.

Items most like this one, by meaning rather than by words (AC-108).

"Like" here is a vector neighbourhood, which is a different question from
search: there is no query, so nothing is asked to match, and the answer is
whatever is nearest above a measured floor. Without the floor this would be
the whole corpus in similarity order -- a vector search always has a nearest
neighbour, however unrelated -- and a list that always returns something
teaches its caller to ignore it.

post.description:
Delete several items in one call.

POST rather than DELETE-with-body: DELETE bodies are unevenly supported by
clients and proxies, and an id list can be long enough to matter. The
`:delete` suffix matches the other verb-style routes.

get.description:
Declared jobs, each with its source and last run summary.

Jobs are the durable "collect this source" declarations. Paging is by
offset rather than keyset because the set changes only when a source is
added or deleted, and the order is by id, so a page cannot shift under a
reader the way a newest-first item list can.

parameters.description: Opaque cursor from a previous response.
parameters.name: cursor

schema.description: Opaque cursor from a previous response.
schema.title: Cursor

get.description:
Recent runs for one job, newest first.

`error_class` is present only on failures, per the JobRun state machine,
which is what makes a cluster of `structure_changed` visible as the signal
that a source's page shape moved.

A run history is append-at-the-front, so this is keyset-paginated: page two
must not skip a run that started while page one was being read.

parameters.description: Opaque cursor from a previous response.
parameters.name: cursor

schema.description: Opaque cursor from a previous response.
schema.title: Cursor

get.description:
Registered collectors, oldest page first, with manifest and status.

Offset paging with an opaque cursor, the same shape `/v1/sources` uses and
for the same reason: the set is bounded (tens of plugins, and it changes
only on install/uninstall) and the order is stable, so a row cannot shift
under a reader mid-walk. `next_cursor` is what makes a short page honest --
a `limit` that truncates without saying so is silent data loss, which is
the failure this endpoint's bound exists to avoid (issue #68).

delete.description:
Remove an installed plugin from the registry, leaving its files.

The files are the operator's, not the host's: deleting them would fuse a
reversible act (uninstall) with an irreversible one (deleting data).

Refused while the plugin still serves an active source -- pulling a
collector out from under its sources would make them fail on the next
tick with a classification that blamed the origin.

post.description:
Install a plugin from the plugin directory.

The work, in order: read and validate the manifest, then verify *in a
child process* that the plugin's code provides what the manifest
declares. Running the check in a child is what keeps the host from
executing a plugin's top-level code, and it is also the only way to know
the plugin is importable before it is recorded as installed.

Pick up edited plugin code without restarting the service.

A child is killed and respawned rather than reloaded in place, which is
what makes this safe where the on-disk reload of a shipped collector is
not (ADR 0017): the plugin's state lives in its own process, and the host
keeps none.

get.description:
List sources, oldest page first by creation order.

Offset paging, unlike the items endpoint's keyset cursor. Sources are
bounded (an operator's subscriptions, tens not millions) and new ones are
appended at the end of this ordering, so a row arriving mid-walk shifts
nothing already read -- the failure offset paging is famous for needs
insertion *ahead* of the cursor, which is what items do and sources do not.
The cursor is opaque to clients either way, so switching to keyset later
would not be a breaking change.

post.description:
Add a source to collect.

Returns the existing source when this URL is already known, rather than an
error: the operation is "make sure this is subscribed", and a retry after a
dropped response must not fail.

delete.description:
Delete a source and everything it collected (ADR 0021).

Destructive and not reversible: the source row, its items, their bodies,
their read state and processor products, and the fetch records all go. The
endpoint used to be a soft delete that left the source as a tombstone with
its items published; that is no longer what this means, and any caller
relying on the old behaviour is relying on something the API does not
promise.

Deleting an id that is already gone answers 200 with `sources: 0` rather
than 404. A client retrying a request whose response was lost cannot tell
"it was here and I removed it" from "it was never here", and after the
first call those are the same fact.

patch.description: Change a source's schedule policy, status or trust level.

get.description:
Processor-chain rows for one source: the agent's visibility into
what the chain is doing and why an item is being held.

Bounded like every other list route. This one had no bound at all, which
was survivable only while the MCP wrapper cut every list to 20; once the
wrapper stopped overruling the requested page (issue #65), an unbounded
`data` here would have been the one way a result set could still grow
without anyone asking. `total` counts every match, so a short page is
announced rather than implied.

post.description:
Delete a source's items, keeping the source itself.

The "this crawl was wrong, keep collecting" case. The source keeps its
cursor, so the subscription resumes rather than re-sampling history
(ADR 0021).

`include_published` defaults true: the caller has explicitly asked to
clear this source's contents, and silently keeping the items every client
has already cached would leave a source that looks emptied while its
articles are still everywhere.

Queue processor products for items stored before the chain was enabled.

A write (it mutates item_enrichment and spends provider budget), so it is
authenticated, idempotent and audited like every other write.

The batch size defaults to a conservative limit; see
`BackfillChainRequest`. Unbounded was how one call turned into 122 fetches
of a single blog, so the default is now something an operator can watch.

get.description:
Everything one question needs: why is this source not updating?

Declared *before* `GET /sources/{source_id}` on purpose: that route's path
parameter matches `:diagnose` too, and Starlette takes the first route that
matches, so the other order answers 404 with `source_id` set to
"abc:diagnose". The POST verbs elsewhere in this module do not have the
problem because no GET route can shadow them.

An aggregate endpoint rather than six calls, which is ADR 0036's rule for a
question that is always asked the same way: the source's own state, its job
and recent runs with their error classes, how much is stuck behind its
processing chain, and whether the collection loop is alive at all. The order
those calls go in is knowledge the caller should not have to have, and
stopping after two of them produces a confident answer built from half the
evidence.

`get_source` remains the full single row; this is the diagnostic view.

post.description:
Fetch one address into one source, and answer with a receipt.

The atom the plural forms are made of: `POST /v1/sources/{id}:fetch-items`
loops it, and `POST /v1/works` with `kind=fetch` runs it once per target.
One implementation (`pipeline.fetch_one`) behind all three is what keeps
"the same address gives the same identity and the same outcome" true
however it was asked for -- and what keeps the host check, the capability
check and the dedupe from existing in three versions.

The answer is one receipt, never a list: a response cannot be smaller than
the effect it reports, and the effect here is one address. Two refusals are
the *source's* rather than the address's, and both happen before anything
is fetched -- an inactive source (409) and a collector without the item
capability (422) -- because nothing about this address could have made them
work. An address off the source's host is not a refusal: it is a receipt
with `outcome=rejected`, because that is what happened to it.

What it did is written down before the receipt is built: a one-target work
and its unit, created and closed in the same transaction (by then the fetch
has happened), so the receipt is also a ledger row. "What happened to this
address?" therefore survives the response: `GET /v1/items?url=` answers for
the item and `GET /v1/works/{id}/units` for the attempt.

Fetch a caller's addresses into one source, reporting each outcome.

**Deprecated**: the list runs inside this request and the answer carries one
result per address, so the response's size follows its input. Two hundred
addresses time out at the gateway while the deployment keeps fetching, and
the results die with the response that carried them. `POST /v1/works` with
`kind=fetch` is the replacement -- it answers with a handle, and
`GET /v1/works/{id}/units` is where the per-address results live, so they
survive a timeout and can be re-read. This endpoint stays for callers that
already use it, limited to `MAX_COMPAT_FETCH_ITEMS` addresses: a batch small
enough to answer inline.

The service side of content-level discovery: the caller (an agent, usually)
enumerates *addresses* -- which this deployment cannot do without crawling
the site -- and the source's own collector fetches them. The site's
knowledge stays in the collector, and every item still lands through the
one write path (normalise -> dedupe -> gate), which is why this is not the
same thing as `POST /v1/sources/{id}:ingest`: there the caller fetched, and
the source is an `agent` source holding content from outside this
deployment's reach.

Two refusals happen before anything is fetched, because nothing about the
list could have made them work: a collector without the item capability
(422), and a list over this endpoint's ceiling (422, pointing at
`/v1/works`).

The run is recorded in the work ledger before the response is built, so
"what happened to this address?" stays answerable later even though this
response is itself a report. That work is written **terminal** -- by then
the fetch has happened -- so it never occupies the live-command index and
no worker can pick it up; a compat run that dies mid-flight therefore
leaves no row, which is one more reason to move to `/v1/works`, where the
row is written before the fetch.

Push items into an agent source (A3, ADR 0022).

The draft is built here and handed to `normalise_and_store`, the same call
a collector's parse output takes. Everything downstream -- sanitising at
the store boundary, content-addressed storage, the six-way dedupe, the
publish gate -- is therefore shared with collection rather than
reimplemented, which is the whole point of the design: a second writer
would either bypass sanitisation or force it to be duplicated.

Scope is `ingest`: a credential that can push content is not automatically
one that can delete sources, rewrite schedules or read anyone's state. The
full token holds both, so this narrows the *ingest* credential rather than
the full one (ADR 0022).

Items are visible on submit when the source has no chain, matching a
chainless rss source. The user's decision (2026-09-14) was explicit that
agent content should be visible without a hold-back step.

get.description:
What this source's chain is doing, in one constant-size answer.

The counts are a fold over the chain rows -- the same rows
`/v1/sources/{id}/enrichments` renders -- so the two cannot disagree; the
rate is derived from the completion timestamps in a window, never stored
(ADR 0009's rule about `next_run_time`, applied to a statistic). Together
they answer "how much is waiting, and is it draining?", which used to cost
one call per source: a measured backlog check across 82 sources was 82
requests, and none of them said how fast anything was moving.

`oldest_queued_at` is what counts cannot say: a queue of one that has been
waiting an hour is a different problem from a queue of one that just
arrived.

post.description:
Requeue failed enrichment rows for one source.

This is the manual/agent re-trigger the retry policy stops at: rows that
exhausted their attempts, or failed non-transiently (auth after a key
rotation, parse on a content shape since fixed), come back as queued and
the worker charges the provider again. A write for that reason.

Collect a source now.

Runs in the request rather than returning 202 with a job id: P1 has no
worker, and the handler is `def` so the event loop stays free while it
runs. The scheduler work replaces this with a durable job; until then a
promise that could be lost to a restart would be worse than a slower
answer that is true.

Add several sources in one request, reporting each item's outcome.

The batch primitive behind MCP's `add_sources` (ADR 0044). Shared options
apply to every URL, and `type: 'auto'` is resolved per URL. A URL that
cannot be used fails alone -- the rest are still created -- because
refusing the whole list over one typo is the loop this endpoint replaces.

Answers 200 with per-item results rather than 201: the body is a report
about a list, and some of it may have failed.

get.description:
Compact system state, sized to be pasted into a conversation.

Reports the decay signals architecture section 7.7 names — error
distribution, the pending backlog, recent success rate — rather than a
wall of counters, because the point is noticing that something is going
wrong, not counting rows.

post.description:
Accept a batch of work; answer with a handle, not with a report.

Answers 202 rather than 200 because the work has not happened yet: it is
queued, and `Location` names where its status lives.

get.description:
One work: its status, its command, and the folded counts.

Deliberately **not** the target list: a 1000-target work must not put 1000
strings into a response that is meant to be O(1), and the caller already
has what it submitted. The enumeration is `/units`, which pages.

The per-target ledger: what happened to each target, paged.

This is the read that replaces the report the old endpoint returned inline.
Because it is a query rather than a response, it survives the client timing
out, it can be re-read later, and `outcome=failed` answers "what do I need
to re-send?" in one call -- a question that had no answer once the response
carrying it was lost.
